summary:
Me (Christopher), and my good friend Gurneik B. have come together to create Earth Radio. Earth Radio is an interactive globe that lets people explore NASA Earth visualizations through sound. Choose one of 12 regional stations and listen to three original arrangements shaped in real time by the imagery: ocean currents, night lights, aerosols, and more. As the visual frames change, their brightness, colour, contrast, and motion influence synthesized notes, textures, and rhythmic accents.

A guided comparison lets listeners hear how brighter and darker areas of the same NASA night-light frame affect the sound. Source controls make it possible to explore individual layers and read how each mapping works. Keyboard navigation, a searchable station list, transcripts, and reduced-motion options offer different ways to engage.

Created for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, Earth Radio turns NASA imagery into an exploratory listening experience for curious people, classrooms, and museums. Its sound is an artistic interpretation of historical and modeled visualizations, not a live feed or calibrated measurement.
details:
Earth Radio turns NASA Earth visualizations into a radio you can explore. Rotate the globe or search for a place, choose a station, and press Play. Each of the 12 stations has three arrangements, giving listeners 36 tracks that bring together imagery from oceans, cities, forests, and the atmosphere. A source window shows the NASA visualization behind the experience and links back to its original page.

How the sound works

The browser samples small regions of NASA visualization frames and measures features such as brightness, colour, contrast, and changes between frames. Those features shape synthesized tones, filters, textures, and rhythmic accents in real time. For example, brighter pixels in a night-light map influence glass-like notes, while changes in ocean frames shape the pulse. Each station also has authored motifs and a rhythmic structure, so the result is a musical arrangement informed by the images rather than a direct recording of Earth.

Explore the sources

A station can combine several NASA layers. Listeners can inspect the original source frames, move the image focus, and hear one sound layer on its own or return to the full mix. The guided listen compares two regions of the same frozen Black Marble frame: a darker Pacific window and a brighter region around the Mediterranean and North Africa. Both use the same instrument and mapping, making it easier to hear how rendered brightness changes the notes.

The project uses NASA Scientific Visualization Studio media including ECCO ocean currents, Perpetual Ocean 2, Black Marble night lights, historical lightning, GEOS aerosols and PM2.5, GEDI forest height, and modeled carbon dioxide. NASA Blue Marble provides the globe base. Some moving-camera ocean and atmospheric-river clips are visual context only. Source pages, credits, dates, and mapping explanations are available in the app.

Accessible exploration and scientific care

Earth Radio is designed to offer another way to engage with Earth science, including for people who may prefer listening alongside visual exploration. It includes keyboard navigation, a searchable station list, text descriptions, transcripts for optional host introductions, playback and volume controls, and reduced-motion support. We hope it can encourage curiosity in classrooms, museums, and independent exploration; its educational and accessibility outcomes have not yet been studied with users.

The sounds are interpretations of rendered image pixels, not calibrated measurements or field recordings. Source images come from different historical periods and models; they are not synchronized observations or a live feed. The aerosol layer is a still. Camera movement, labels, colour choices, and compression can affect what is sampled, and station pins represent broad editorial regions rather than sensors.

Technology and credits

We built the application with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, Web Audio, and a custom WebGL globe with a Canvas fallback. Music is synthesized in the browser; no AI model or external audio service is called during playback. OpenAI Codex assisted with coding, design research, testing, and documentation; Claude reviewed an earlier snapshot. Optional station introductions are prerecorded synthetic narration generated with ElevenLabs. NASA imagery is attributed to its original sources, and NASA does not endorse Earth Radio.

Further work includes testing with blind and low-vision users, scientific and audio review, improving geographic registration, and checking performance on physical phones and additional browsers.
